summary: Joey Hung studied at the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts and works in Buddhist studies, holding a post at the Dharma Drum Institute of Liberal Arts.
Jogendra Singh is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology who studied at Nava Nalanda Mahavihara under Uma Shankar Vyas.

Jogindra Nath Samaddar, an Indologist and historian educated at Bangabasi College and Presidency College, Chennai, taught at St. Columba's College (~1908–1917), Patna College (1912), Pramatha-Manmatha College, and Patna University (1923).

Johan Elverskog specializes in Buddhist, Iranian, Central Asian, and religious studies. Educated at UC Berkeley (B.A. ~1989–1993) and Indiana University (M.A. ~1993–1995), he became Dedman Family Distinguished Professor at Southern Methodist University around 2002.

Johan Hendrik Caspar Kern was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Utrecht, Leiden, and under Albrecht Weber. He taught at Government Sanskrit College, Varanasi (~1863–1865), and held the Chair of Sanskrit at Leiden University (1865–1903).
Johan Hendrik Kern was a linguist who held posts at the University of Groningen from 1901 to 1924 and at Leiden University from 1924 to 1933.

Historian and Indologist Johan Huizinga studied at Groningen and Leiden, learning from Johan Hendrik Caspar Kern. He later held academic posts at the University of Groningen (1905–1915) and Leiden University (1914–1942).

Johann Andreas Schmeller studied at the Wilhelmsgymnasium. He taught at the Bavarian Cadet Corps (~1817–1827), served as Kustos at the Bavarian State Library from 1829, and held a chair at the University of Munich starting in 1828 and 1846.

Johann Caspar von Orelli was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He held positions at the Cantonal School of Graubünden (~1807–1819), the Carolinum Zürich (~1819–1833), and the University of Zurich (~1833–1849).

Johann Christoph Adelung was a linguist educated at the University of Halle (~1750–1753). He served as a professor at Evangelisches Ratsgymnasium Erfurt (1758) and as principal librarian for the Electorate of Saxony in Dresden (1787–1806).
Johann Elias Schlegel studied at Schulpforta (~1733–1739) and the University of Leipzig (~1739–1742).
Johann Friedrich Blumenbach studied at the University of Jena (~1769–1772) and the University of Göttingen (~1772–1775), where he subsequently held a faculty post from around 1776 to 1840.
Johann Friedrich Herbart was a philosopher who studied at the University of Jena (~1794–1797) and held a post at the University of Göttingen from around 1802 to 1809.

Johann Friedrich Pfaff studied at Karlsschule Stuttgart and the University of Göttingen (1785–1787). He held academic posts at the University of Helmstedt (1788–1810) and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (1810–1825).

Indologist Johann Gildemeister studied at Göttingen and Bonn under Heinrich Ewald, Georg Wilhelm Freytag, Christian Lassen, and A. W. von Schlegel. He held professorships at the University of Marburg (~1845–1859) and the University of Bonn (~1859–1890).

Johann Gottfried Eichhorn, working in religious studies, history, and linguistics, studied at Göttingen under Christian Gottlob Heyne (1770–1774). He served as professor of oriental languages at Jena (1775) and professor of philosophy at Göttingen (1788).

Indologist and linguist Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten studied at Greifswald and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He held professorships at the University of Jena (1817–1824) and the University of Greifswald (1824–1850).

Johann Gottfried von Herder, active in philosophy and linguistics, studied theology at Königsberg (1761). He taught at Riga Cathedral School (1764–1769) and later served as General Superintendent and gymnasium director in Saxe-Weimar from 1776.

Johann Gustav Stickel, a scholar of linguistics and Iranian/Central Asian studies, studied at Jena under Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten and in Paris under Silvestre de Sacy, later serving as professor at Jena (1830–1836).
Johann Jakob Engel was a philosopher who studied at the University of Rostock (~1757–1762) and the University of Leipzig (~1762–1765).
